title: When it rains
tomorrow: a friend is in the hospital. what do you actually say?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the new moon: a month greeted like a guest, with a request for safety and faith. Today, weather.

Here's a strange pair of requests, both in the hadith collection of al-Bukhari, both made during Friday sermons, one Friday apart. First, a man stands up while the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is preaching. The animals are dying, the roads are cut, he says. Pray for rain. The Prophet raises his hands and prays, and the rain comes, and keeps coming until the next Friday. Then a man stands up again. Now the houses are falling and the roads are cut. Pray for it to stop. Same sky. Same water. Opposite prayers. So which one was right?
screen: `PRAY FOR RAIN.` → `THE RAIN DOESN'T STOP.` → `PRAY FOR IT TO MOVE.` → `WHICH ONE WAS RIGHT?`

segments.voice: Both, and the second answer is the clue. The Prophet doesn't pray the rain away. He raises his hands and asks: around us, not on us. On the hills, the valleys, the places where trees grow. The rain isn't canceled; it's moved to where it can help. Now the short line Muslims say when rain begins, also in al-Bukhari, makes sense. It's two words in Arabic: sayyiban nafi'an. A pouring rain, a beneficial one. That second word does all the work. Rain on its own isn't simply good or bad. The same storm fills a farmer's well and floods a basement. So the prayer doesn't just ask for more of a thing. It asks for the kind that does good. Then there's one more detail, from Sahih Muslim, the kind you'd tell a friend tonight. Once, when rain began, the Prophet pulled back part of his garment so the drops would land on him. Asked why, he said, in effect: it has just come from its Lord. He wanted to feel it fresh, the way a kid runs out into the first rain of the year. So the rain is welcomed with the skin, asked for with open hands, and redirected when it harms, with the same Lord addressed every time. That's the puzzle solved: nobody in the story was asking God for weather. They were asking for benefit, and benefit sometimes means less.
screen: `AROUND US, NOT ON US.` · `SAYYIBAN NAFI'AN: A BENEFICIAL RAIN.` · `THE SAME STORM, TWO OUTCOMES.` · `FRESH FROM ITS LORD.` · then, large: `BENEFICIAL RAIN.`

segments.voice: Find the nearest sound of water: rain on a window, a running tap, a kettle starting to hum. Listen to it for the whole sit, and let the two words ride on it if you like: sayyiban nafi'an.
When it rains. Muslims say sayyiban nafi'an, a beneficial rain: asking not for more weather, but for the kind that helps.
The line for today: beneficial rain: not more of it, the good kind. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: When rain begins, many Muslims say the Prophet's words from al-Bukhari, sayyiban nafi'an (a beneficial rain); when rain does harm, some say his other words, around us, not on us.

match.prompt: the rain puzzle — tap the pairs.

fork.setup: your town's been in drought for months, and the forecast finally shows a huge storm with flood warnings. what fits the rain prayer best?
options: ask that it rain hard enough to end the drought, whatever it costs.
ask for the rain, and that it fall where it helps and not where it harms.
don't ask for anything; the weather isn't a thing to pray about.
fork.reveal: a beneficial rain, and around us, not on us: the Prophet asked for rain, and asked for it to land where it does good.

original.note: Arabic: nafi', beneficial, useful. In the rain prayer: sayyiban nafi'an, a beneficial downpour.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prayer for rain is a prayer for more rain.
what it means: sayyiban nafi'an asks for rain that does good, and 'around us, not on us' moves harmful rain to where it helps.

what a scholar hears: two Friday sermons in al-Bukhari's book of rain prayers, one asking for rain and one for its redirection, and a Muslim hadith of the Prophet baring himself to rain 'fresh from its Lord'.
guess: a short prayer asking for rain that does good
a prayer asking God to hold back a coming storm
a thank-you said after the rain has stopped

chat.says: storm canceled my campus tour AND flooded the street by dad's shop. so is rain a blessing or not??
options: The prayer asks for beneficial rain. Same storm, different results; you ask for the good kind.
Always a blessing. If it flooded the street, that's on the city, not the rain.
Not this time. The prayer is really for farms, so city rain doesn't count.
chat.meaning: Muslims ask for sayyiban nafi'an, a beneficial rain. The same storm can help or harm, so the prayer asks for the kind that does good.

al-Bukhari.meaning: a classical hadith scholar; his Sahih collection keeps the rain prayers

sayyiban nafi'an.meaning: a pouring rain, a beneficial one

Sahih Muslim.meaning: a classical hadith collection, compiled by Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1032 (sayyiban nafi'an, on seeing rain)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1013–1014 (the Friday request for rain, and the next Friday's 'around us, not on us')
Sahih Muslim 898 (rain 'recently come from its Lord')

notes: Bukhari 1032 (sayyiban nafi'an) paraphrased; confirm number and wording.

Bukhari 1013–1014 (the man at the Friday sermon; rain until the next Friday; 'around us, not on us', on hills, valleys and where trees grow): paraphrased. Some narrations say the same man returned, some say 'a man'; the script says 'a man stands up again'. Confirm numbers.
Muslim 898: the Prophet uncovered part of his garment so rain would fall on him, saying it had recently come from its Lord; paraphrased 'in effect'. Confirm.
